basis: Independently curated original deck retained in full, with original note-based additions reviewed against the subject specification. External notes supply coverage prompts, not verbatim cards.

base_cards.front: What is an air mass?
back: A large body of air with similar temperature and moisture.

base_cards.front: Which air mass usually brings mild, wet weather from the Atlantic?
back: Tropical maritime.

base_cards.front: What is continentality?
back: The effect of distance from the sea on climate.

base_cards.front: Give one renewable energy source.
back: Wind power.

base_cards.front: What gas makes biogas useful as a fuel?
back: Methane.

base_cards.front: Name the UK flood case study used in this course.
back: Somerset Levels.

base_cards.front: Explain how the North Atlantic Drift affects the UK climate.
back: It transfers warm ocean water towards north-west Europe.
This helps make UK winters milder than places at a similar latitude.

base_cards.front: Explain why western uplands are generally wetter than eastern lowlands.
back: Moist Atlantic air is forced to rise over upland relief.
It cools, condenses and produces rainfall before descending towards the east.

base_cards.front: Give two effects of flooding on people.
back: Homes or businesses may be damaged.
Roads may be cut off, disrupting travel and services.

base_cards.front: Give one advantage and one disadvantage of a reservoir.
back: Advantage: it stores water for periods of high demand or low rainfall.
Disadvantage: it floods land and can damage habitats or communities.

base_cards.front: Explain why wind power needs support from storage or other energy sources.
back: Wind speed varies, so output is intermittent.
Supply must still meet demand when turbines generate little electricity.

base_cards.front: Give two products of anaerobic digestion.
back: Biogas.
Digestate.

base_cards.front: Explain how prolonged rainfall can cause river flooding.
back: Rain fills soil stores until the ground becomes saturated.
More water then flows over the surface or rapidly through the soil into rivers.
Discharge rises above channel capacity and water spills onto the floodplain.

base_cards.front: Explain why the Somerset Levels are vulnerable to flooding.
back: The landscape is very low and flat; about 18% of Somerset lies below average high-tide level.
Water drains slowly through rivers and artificial channels, especially when the ground is saturated.
High tides can restrict river outflow, so water spreads widely across the Levels.

base_cards.front: Explain one environmental problem caused by intensive food production.
back: Large fertiliser inputs can be washed into rivers.
Nutrients encourage excessive algal growth.
Decomposition then reduces oxygen, harming aquatic life.

base_cards.front: Explain how anaerobic digestion produces useful energy.
back: Microorganisms break down organic material in a sealed tank without oxygen.
This releases methane-rich biogas.
The gas is burned in suitable equipment to produce heat or electricity.

base_cards.front: Explain how air masses and continentality create contrasting UK weather.
back: Tropical maritime air crosses the Atlantic and brings mild, moist conditions.
Polar continental air can bring cold, dry conditions from eastern Europe.
Coastal places are moderated by the sea because water heats and cools slowly.
Inland areas have a greater temperature range because land changes temperature faster.

base_cards.front: Explain how two long-term strategies reduce flood risk on the Somerset Levels.
back: Dredging selected sections of the Parrett and Tone increases channel capacity; programmes in 2014, 2016 and 2018 removed about 270,500 m³ of silt.
Raising the Muchelney–Drayton road maintains community access during floods, reducing isolation even when surrounding land stores water.

base_cards.front: Explain why the UK's energy mix has changed since 1950.
back: Domestic coal declined as mines closed and pollution and carbon concerns grew.
Oil and gas became important for transport, heating and electricity.
Nuclear provided dependable low-operational-carbon electricity.
Falling costs, technology and climate policy encouraged growth in renewables.

base_cards.front: Explain two disadvantages of Hinkley Point C.
back: A very large, lengthy construction project creates traffic, accommodation pressure, cost and local habitat or landscape disturbance.
Radioactive waste from electricity generation must be securely managed for far longer than the station's planned 60-year operating life.

additions.front: Why can polar continental air bring snow after crossing the North Sea?
back: It begins cold and relatively dry, but can gain moisture over the sea. That moisture can produce wintry precipitation when it reaches the UK.

additions.front: How does continentality affect the annual temperature range?
back: Land heats and cools faster than sea. Inland places tend to have a greater seasonal range, while coastal water moderates temperature.

additions.front: Why are western UK uplands often wetter?
back: Moist Atlantic air is forced upwards by high land. It cools, water vapour condenses and relief rainfall forms.

additions.front: Does a rainy national climate mean every UK region has enough water?
back: No. Rainfall, storage and demand vary by place and season. A densely populated region can face pressure despite the national climate being wet.

additions.front: How can heavy farm machinery increase runoff?
back: It can compact soil, reducing infiltration. More rainfall then travels over the surface rather than entering the soil.

additions.front: How can fertiliser runoff harm a river?
back: Extra nutrients can encourage algal growth. Decomposition uses oxygen, which can harm aquatic organisms.

additions.front: How can commercial fishing damage more than the target fish stock?
back: Some methods disturb the seabed or catch unwanted species. Taking breeding fish too quickly also reduces future stock recovery.

additions.front: What is the main trade-off in a water-transfer scheme?
back: It can supply an area of high demand, but building and pumping require resources. Excessive removal may harm the source area and its ecosystems.

additions.front: How does energy security differ from simply owning fuel reserves?
back: Secure energy must be dependable and affordable when needed. Extraction, infrastructure, costs and disruptions matter as well as reserves.

additions.front: Why can UK gas prices change after decisions made in other countries?
back: The UK trades in interconnected energy markets. Overseas production decisions or disrupted supplies can affect the price of imported fuel.

additions.front: What does OPEC help explain in an energy-supply answer?
back: Oil-producing countries can influence world supply through production decisions, which can affect prices and importing countries.

additions.front: What does fracking do to shale rock?
back: High-pressure fluid creates fractures. Sand helps keep openings available so trapped gas can flow towards the well.

additions.front: Give two environmental costs of fracking beyond the visual effect.
back: It uses water and produces wastewater needing management. Methane leakage and carbon dioxide from burning the gas contribute to climate effects; induced seismic activity is another concern.

additions.front: Why is domestic shale gas not a renewable energy resource?
back: It is a finite fossil fuel formed over geological time. Producing it within the UK changes the source of supply, not whether it is replenished.

additions.front: How does energy efficiency differ from conservation?
back: Efficiency provides a similar service with less energy, such as improved insulation. Conservation reduces unnecessary use, such as switching off unused lights.

additions.front: Why should the UK energy-usage table not be read as an electricity-generation table?
back: Primary energy use includes transport, heating and inputs to electricity production. Electricity generation describes only one part of the energy system.

additions.front: What is lag time on a storm hydrograph?
back: The time between peak rainfall and peak river discharge, not the time from the first raindrop to the end of flooding.

additions.front: Why did pumping not instantly solve the 2013–14 Somerset flooding?
back: A very large volume of water occupied low-lying land, while high river and tidal levels restricted drainage. Pumps worked within those physical limits.

additions.front: Why is Hinkley Point C’s planned output different from a current operating benefit?
back: It remains under construction in this case-study account. Planned generation becomes available only after completion and operation, while construction jobs and disruption occur earlier.

additions.front: What are the two useful material and energy routes at Dryholme Farm?
back: Biogas is burned to provide energy, while digestate returns nutrients to farmland. Digestate itself is not the fuel supplied to the engine.
